result: Bdf1/2 have important TFIID-independent contributions to transcription, with many genes being more sensitive to Bdf1/2 depletion than to TFIID depletion. Depletion of both Bdf1 and Bdf2 results in a global collapse of transcription with median decreases of ~4-5.4-fold, and 68% of TFIID-dependent genes are more sensitive to Bdf than Taf1 depletion.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C59, C60, C72, C77, C78, C80, C88, C89, and C181 are supported by RNA-seq data comparing Bdf1/2 and TFIID depletion effects (Figure 1A-C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F). The data show global transcription collapse upon Bdf1/2 depletion and differential sensitivity of genes to Bdf versus TFIID depletion, with appropriate controls and replicates (CV <30% for nearly all experiments).

result: Bdf1/2 co-occupy the majority of yeast promoters with similar binding patterns to TFIID. ChEC-seq identified 3700, 3466, and 3103 promoters bound by Bdf1, Bdf2, and Taf1, respectively, with extensive overlap between Bdf1 and Bdf2 binding and between Bdf1 and Taf1 binding.
evaluation: Claims C8, C99-C106, and C187 are supported by ChEC-seq data (Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B). The genome-wide mapping shows characteristic binding patterns and extensive overlap between factors, validated by orthogonal ChIP-seq approach (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E). Peak calling and correlation analyses support the conclusions about co-occupancy.

result: Bdf1/2 affect preinitiation complex formation through recruitment of TFIID, Mediator, and basal transcription factors to chromatin. Bdf depletion causes modest (~1.7-fold) decreases in TFIID and Mediator occupancy, but these decreases are significantly stronger than those caused by depleting Med14 or Taf13, indicating independent contributions of Bdfs beyond cooperative interactions between TFIID and Mediator.
evaluation: Claims C9, C61, C132, C133, C136-C141, C196, and C198 are supported by ChEC-seq and ChIP-seq data (Figure 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-F). The comparative analysis of factor depletion effects shows that Bdfs have independent contributions to recruitment of both TFIID and Mediator, with appropriate controls and correlation analyses between different subunits of the same complex.

result: Hypersensitivity of genes to Bdf1/2 depletion results from combined defects in transcription initiation and early elongation. At the most Bdf-dependent genes, transcription defects significantly exceed defects in TFIIB and Pol II binding, while at the least Bdf-dependent genes, more efficient elongation partially nullifies initiation defects.
evaluation: Claims C10, C62, C63, C145-C147, C165-C167, and C171 are supported by combined analysis of RNA-seq, ChIP-seq for TFIIB and Pol II, and CTD phosphorylation data (Figures 5C, 6A-E). The disproportionate transcription defects compared to factor binding defects, changes in Pol II distribution, traveling ratio analysis, and CTD phosphorylation patterns provide converging evidence for combined initiation and elongation defects. The TFIID-independence is validated by comparison with Taf1 depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-D).

result: Bdf1/2 have striking functional similarity to human BET proteins, most notably Brd4. Phylogenetic analysis shows Bdf1 BDs are more closely related to Brd4 than hTaf1 BDs, conserved domains show ≥50% similarity, TATA-less genes in both systems are more affected by BET depletion, and there is extensive overlap in gene ontology terms. Both yeast and human BET proteins are involved in Mediator recruitment and modulation of transcriptional elongation.
evaluation: Claims C11, C64, C95-C98, C182-C183, C209, C236-C239 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1D-E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), comparative RNA-seq analysis between yeast and human systems (Figure 1F), gene ontology analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), and functional data showing similar roles in Mediator recruitment and elongation. The comparative analysis is strengthened by citations to prior human BET literature showing similar elongation defects.

result: Depletion of either Bdfs or Taf13 causes global loss of TFIIB, most pronounced at TFIID-dependent promoters. Bdf depletion causes significantly larger loss of TFIIB at TFIID-dependent promoters than TFIID depletion, while at CR genes, TFIID depletion causes greater loss in TFIIB signal.
evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are supported by ChIP-seq data for TFIIB (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The comparative analysis shows differential effects of Bdf versus TFIID depletion on TFIIB binding at different gene classes, with appropriate statistical testing and replicates.

result: The change in transcription following Bdf depletion is not proportional to the loss of Pol II signal. Bdf depletion causes differential effects on Pol II distribution along genes, with increased loss downstream of TSS at the most Bdf-dependent genes and partial recovery at the least Bdf-dependent genes. Changes in traveling ratio correlate with changes in transcription and TFIIB loss.
evaluation: Claims C153-C164 are supported by Pol II ChIP-seq data (Figure 6A-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C). The analysis of Pol II distribution, traveling ratio calculations, and correlation analyses provide evidence for differential elongation effects. The specificity to Bdf depletion is validated by comparison with Taf1 depletion showing no similar changes.

result: At the most Bdf-dependent genes, Pol II becomes hypophosphorylated on Ser2 and Ser5 after depleting Bdfs, while at the least Bdf-dependent genes, Pol II becomes weakly hyperphosphorylated. Similar changes were not observed after Taf1 depletion.
evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are supported by CTD phosphorylation ChIP-seq data (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D). The differential phosphorylation patterns at different gene classes and the lack of similar changes after Taf1 depletion validate the TFIID-independent role of Bdfs in elongation. The data are consistent with the traveling ratio and Pol II distribution analyses.

result: The relative gene body occupancies of Bur1 and Ctk1, but not Spt5, correlate with gene dependence on Bdfs. After Bdf depletion, Bur1 and Ctk1 occupancy relative to Rpb1 increases at all genes, with the largest increases at the most Bdf-dependent genes, despite decreased CTD Ser2 phosphorylation. These results indicate that changes in kinase recruitment cannot account for Bdf function in elongation, and the elongation defect is restricted to the first ~400 bp of the transcribed region.
evaluation: Claims C174-C180 are supported by ChIP-seq data for Bur1, Ctk1, and Spt5 (Figure 6F-G, Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The paradoxical increase in kinase occupancy despite decreased CTD phosphorylation is well-documented and provides strong evidence that Bdf function in elongation is not mediated through kinase recruitment. The spatial restriction of the defect to ~400 bp is consistent across multiple analyses.

result: Esa1 depletion reveals a global loss of transcription with good but nonlinear correlation with Bdf experiment (r = 0.73). Bdf depletion results in stronger transcriptional defects than Esa1 depletion, suggesting a portion of Bdf function is H4Ac independent. After Esa1 depletion, H4K12ac signal decreases dramatically but Bdf1 remains bound at substantial levels, especially at promoters.
evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and ChEC-seq data (Figure 3A-E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D). The comparative analysis shows that Bdf function extends beyond H4 acetylation recognition, with Bdf1 remaining bound after loss of H4K12ac. The correlation between Bdf1 promoter signal changes and transcription changes following Esa1 depletion supports the conclusion that Esa1 effects are largely mediated by Bdf1.

result: Yeast BET proteins Bdf1 and Bdf2 are functionally redundant under normal growth conditions, with Bdf1 being the dominant factor. Bdf1 was efficiently degraded (<10% remaining) while Bdf2 degradation was less complete (~15% remaining). Bdf2 degradation or deletion showed minimal transcription changes while Bdf1 degradation resulted in modest defects. Changes in transcription following Bdf1 or Bdf1/2 depletion are highly correlated (r = 0.82-0.95), and Bdf1 and Bdf2 have nearly identical genome-wide binding patterns with Bdf2 redistributing from CR to TFIID-dependent genes upon Bdf1 depletion.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46, C65-C68, C70-C71, C73-C74, C227-C231 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), growth assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), RNA-seq data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H), and ChEC-seq data (Figure 2B, E-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). The correlation analyses, binding pattern comparisons, and redistribution data provide strong evidence for functional redundancy with Bdf1 dominance.

result: For both TFIID-dependent and CR gene classes, normalized H4K12ac levels at promoters significantly differ depending on Bdf1 peak presence. Following Bdf1 depletion, Bdf2 signal increases at TFIID promoters at the expense of CR promoters, with changes correlating with gene dependence on Bdfs (r = -0.52). Bdf1 does not redistribute in response to Bdf2 depletion.
evaluation: Claims C113-C118 are supported by ChIP-seq data for H4K12ac (Figure 2D) and ChEC-seq data for Bdf2 redistribution (Figure 2E-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I). The correlation between H4K12ac levels and Bdf1 binding, and the asymmetric redistribution pattern provide evidence for Bdf1 dominance and functional redundancy.

result: Transcription changes upon Bdf or Taf1 depletion correlate but the relationship is not linear. Genes less sensitive to Bdf depletion include almost all CR genes and one-third of TFIID-dependent genes. Nearly all RP genes are significantly less dependent on Bdf1/2 compared with TFIID. Bdf1 and Taf1 are degraded with similar efficiency, and comparison with Taf13 depletion leads to similar conclusions.
evaluation: Claims C75, C76, C79, C81, C83 are supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C) and Western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). The nonlinear relationship and differential gene sensitivities are well-documented, with appropriate controls for protein depletion efficiency.

result: Depletion of basal transcription factors Toa1 or Ssl2 decreases all mRNA transcription independent of gene class with median changes of ~15-fold and ~23-fold, respectively. 38% and 19% of TFIID-dependent genes are similarly sensitive to Toa1 or Ssl2 depletion as they are to Bdf depletion.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1C). The comparison with basal factor depletion provides important context for the magnitude of Bdf effects and validates that Bdf dependence is a good classifier for gene classes.

result: Rapid depletion of H2A.Z did not reveal significant defects in gene transcription, suggesting that global transcriptional defects upon Bdf depletion are not mediated via SWR1 and H2A.Z.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by RNA-seq data following H2A.Z depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E). The lack of transcriptional defects upon H2A.Z depletion provides evidence that Bdf effects on transcription are not mediated through the SWR1 complex, though this is an indirect argument.

result: Bdf1 chromatin occupancy is only weakly predictive of gene dependence on Bdf1/2, similar to human BET factors. Bdf1 ChIP-seq results are similar to ChEC-seq and previously published ChIP-exo data, though ChIP-seq detects fewer bound promoters due to worse signal-to-background ratio. A major difference between ChEC-seq and ChIP-seq was observed at RP genes, with 15% detected by ChEC-seq versus 94% by ChIP-seq.
evaluation: Claims C107-C112 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), comparative analysis of ChEC-seq, ChIP-seq, and ChIP-exo data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-G), and citations to prior human BET literature. The methodological comparison is important for interpreting binding data, and the RP gene discrepancy highlights technical limitations of ChIP-seq.

result: Background knowledge about BET proteins and their roles in transcription. Human BET family members are promising therapeutic targets but their mechanisms are poorly understood. BET proteins have double bromodomains with affinity for hyperacetylated H4, are involved in transcription of most Pol II genes, and Brd4 is most important for transcription changes after BET inactivation. Brd4 contributes to Mediator recruitment, nuclear condensate formation, and productive elongation through unclear mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C34 represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature. These claims provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

result: Background knowledge about yeast TFIID, Bdf1/2, and gene classification. TFIID is a conserved Pol II factor regulating almost all yeast genes. Metazoan TFIID has chromatin readers (Taf1 BD, Taf3 PHD) that are missing in yeast. Bdf1/2 are yeast BET homologs that were previously proposed to target TFIID to acetylated H4, with Bdf1 showing dominant role over Bdf2. Yeast genes can be classified into TFIID-dependent and CR categories based on coactivator requirements.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C35-C43, C47-C58, C90, C93-C94 represent established knowledge and prior work supported by citations. These claims provide essential background for understanding the study's context and rationale. The classification of yeast genes into TFIID-dependent and CR categories is from the authors' prior work.

result: Background knowledge about histone acetylation, elongation factors, and BET protein mechanisms. Esa1 is responsible for H4 acetylation in yeast. Pol II pausing and CTD phosphorylation are important for elongation regulation in metazoans. Bur1/Ctk1 are yeast homologs of Cdk9/Cdk12/13. Various mechanisms have been proposed for BET elongation control including P-TEFb regulation, histone chaperone activity, and kinase activity. Human BET factors show redundancy but Brd4 is most studied.
evaluation: Claims C119, C126-C131, C148-C152, C172-C173, C189-C192, C195, C197, C199-C201, C211, C213-C214, C217, C219-C221, C224-C226, C232-C233, C235 represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature. These claims provide important mechanistic context for interpreting the elongation results.

result: Summary conclusions and interpretations about Bdf1/2 function and BET protein conservation. Bdf1/2 are critical for yeast transcription and provide mechanistic insights into BET function in all eukaryotes. The study proposes that chromatin-tethered BET factors serve as nucleation centers for TFIID and Mediator recruitment, creating a platform for PIC assembly. The role appears widespread and complementary to sequence-specific transcription factors. Cooperation between BET factors and TFIID may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic gene regulation.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C184-C186, C188, C193-C194, C202-C210, C222-C223, C240 represent summary conclusions and mechanistic interpretations based on the experimental data. While the data supporting individual findings are strong, some of the broader mechanistic interpretations (C193, C194, C202, C203) involve speculation about evolutionary conservation and molecular mechanisms that extend beyond the direct experimental evidence. The model is reasonable given the data but represents inference rather than direct demonstration.

result: The variation in nascent mRNA levels between replicate samples was <30% for nearly all experiments.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by coefficient of variation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). This demonstrates good experimental reproducibility and validates the quality of the RNA-seq data.
